Learning Objectives
Identify the pathophysiology, epidemiology, and risk factors associated with anterolateral
bowing and congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia.
Perform an appropriate patient history, physical examination, and imaging workup for
patients in whom congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia is suspected.
Understand the classification of congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia.
Review surgical and nonsurgical treatment principles for patients with anterolateral bowing
and congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia.
Identify the pathophysiology, epidemiology, and risk factors associated with infantile and
adolescent Blount disease.
Understand the classification of Blount disease and its utility in guiding management.
Perform an appropriate patient history, physical examination, and imaging workup for
patients in whom Blount disease is suspected.

Anterolateral Bowing
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Three types of tibial bowing can occur in children, with considerable differences in prognosis
and treatment1 (Table 1).
Anterolateral bowing may progress to congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia (CPT).

Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1423-1436.
Epidemiology
Of patients with anterolateral bowing, 50% have neurofibromatosis.
Of patients with neurofibromatosis, 10% have anterolateral bowing.
CPT occurs in 1 per 140,000 live births.2
Conversely, the incidence of CPT is 1% to 2% in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1).
The deformity in the tibia usually is evident within the patient’s first year of life, with a fracture
commonly occurring by age 2 to 2.5 years.
Etiology
Anterolateral bowing can progress to CPT.
CPT refers to a nonunion of a tibial fracture that develops spontaneously or after trivial trauma
in a dysplastic bone segment of the tibial diaphysis.
The pseudarthrosis usually develops during the first two years of life.
Although the etiologic nature of anterolateral bowing and CPT is unclear, a strong association
exists with NF-1.
A lesser association exists with fibrous dysplasia or osteofibrous dysplasia Campanacci.
Natural History
CPT is one of the most perplexing and challenging orthopaedic problems because of difficulty
attaining union. Union, if achieved, is difficult to maintain.
Spontaneous resolution is unusual.
Good prognostic signs include a duplicated hallux and a delta-shaped osseous segment in the
concavity of the bow.
Fracture risk decreases at skeletal maturity.
Classification
The presence of sclerosis, cysts, fibular dysplasia, and narrowing are the basis of the Boyd and
Crawford classification3 (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Illustrations show the Boyd and Crawford classification of congenital tibial dysplasia.
Type I is characterized by anterior lateral bowing with increased cortical density and a narrow but
normal medullary canal. Type IIA is characterized by anterior lateral bowing with failure of
tubularization and a widened medullary canal. Type IIB is characterized by anterior lateral bowing
with a cystic lesion before fracture or canal enlargement from a previous fracture. Type IIC is
characterized by frank pseudarthrosis and bone atrophy with sucked candy narrowing of the
ends of the two fragments. (Reproduced from Crawford AH, Schorry EK: Neurofibromatosis in
children: The role of the orthopaedist. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1999;7(4):217-230.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History

Patient History
Questioning the patient’s parents about a family history of neurofibromatosis is of
utmost importance to determine if a first-degree relative has NF-1.
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rotational and Angular Limb Deformities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004063
4/22


Physical Examination
A complete physical examination of the patient is required to note other features of NF-
1, which include café-au-lait spots (>5 mm in size in children), inguinal and axillary
freckling (Crowe sign), cutaneous neurofibromas (bluish and raised lesion over skin
surface), Lisch nodules in the eyes, and scoliosis or kyphosis.
Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
Plain AP and lateral radiographs of bilateral tibiae should be obtained for comparison.
Bowing should be identified, and the presence of sclerosis, cysts, fibular dysplasia, and
narrowing should be noted. Depending on these findings, the patient should be followed
every 6 to 12 months with new radiographs to assess the risk of fracture.
Pathology
The main pathology of CPT is hyperplasia of fibroblasts with the formation of dense fibrous
tissue.
The invasive fibromatosis is in the periosteum between broken bone ends and surrounds the
tibia, causing compression, osteolysis, and persistence of the pseudarthrosis.
Management
This condition is difficult to manage because of two factors. The first factor is biologic: poor
healing ability of the dysplastic segment. The second factor is mechanical: technical difficulty of
fixing small and osteopenic bone fragments in children without damaging the distal tibial
physis or ankle.
The initial goal of management is prevention of pseudarthrosis via a clamshell total contact
brace.
If pseudarthrosis develops, all treatment options are associated with more limited success.

Nonsurgical Management
Patients should wear a clamshell total contact brace as soon as they are of weight-bearing age.
By preventing deformity and bowing, the goal of the clamshell brace is to avoid fracture.
Surgical Management
Surgical management of CPT is initiated in patients with a fracture of the tibia or fibula.
Surgical management is performed soon after tibia fracture to avoid complications that result
from delayed management.
Multiple techniques have been described to address the pseudoarthrosis. Regardless of the
method used to manage CPT, the following requirements must be fulfilled to ensure good
results:
Complete excisions of the soft-tissue fibromatosis at the site of the pseudarthrosis with
minimal bony resection
Stimulation of bone healing via autogenous iliac crest bone grafting
Proper fixation of the bone fragments until bone healing is observed on radiographs
Maintenance of bone healing until complete bone consolidation and hypertrophy at the age
of skeletal maturity
Treatment options for pseudarthrosis include any combination of the following:
Intramedullary rod and bone grafting
Intramedullary rod augmented with external fixation (preferred by the author of this lesson)
Intramedullary rod augmented with locked plate
Circular fixator with bone transport
Vascularized fibular graft

Surgical Management
Adjunctive use of bone morphogenetic proteins is an accepted addition to any of the
aforementioned treatment options.
The author of this lesson prefers Ilizarov external fixation augmented by an
intramedullary rod (often a telescopic growing rod). The Ilizarov external fixator
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rotational and Angular Limb Deformities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004063
6/22

facilitates fixation of small bone fragments and compression of the pseudarthrosis. A
locked tibial plate also can be used, with the plate replacing the external fixator.
Recent literature supports the combined use of recombinant bone morphogenic
proteins to augment an autogenous bone graft and postoperative diphosphonates to
enhance bone healing.4
Contraindications
Osteotomies to correct bowing are contraindicated because of the risk of pseudarthrosis of
the osteotomy site.
Postoperative Management

Postoperative Management
After surgical management is complete or the external fixator is removed, the limb is
fitted in a knee-ankle-foot orthosis with a drop lock at the knee and a solid ankle. This
can be gradually changed to a patellar tendon-bearing orthosis if the patient is near
skeletal maturity.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures

Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
The patient is seen at 3 months and at 6 months postoperatively,, and then yearly, with
radiographs obtained at each follow-up visit. Radiographs are obtained to determine
bone quality, evidence of refracture, gradually developing deformity, and the length of
the telescopic intramedullary rod relative to the length of the tibia.
Complications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rotational and Angular Limb Deformities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004063
7/22

Nonunion, malalignment or malunion, refracture, and limb-length discrepancies are common
complications in patients who undergo surgical treatment to correct CPT.
Many children undergo multiple surgical procedures during their growing years to manage this
condition.
Amputation may be considered for persistent pseudarthrosis (usually after two or three failed
surgical procedures). A Syme amputation is preferred to avoid subsequent surgical procedures
for bony stump overgrowth.
Regardless of the surgical procedure performed, some form of bracing is required for all
patients until skeletal maturity to prevent refracture. After patients reach maturity, a
decreased risk for future fracture exists.
Outcomes
Regardless of the treatment option selected, the natural history of CPT is that the affected
bone segment remains atrophic and poorly consolidated with a tendency to refracture until
skeletal maturity. At skeletal maturity, the bone quality becomes almost normal, hypertrophy
of the tibia occurs, and the bone ceases to refracture.
CPT continues to pose a difficult therapeutic challenge in achieving bone healing and
maintaining healing during growth.
Blount Disease (Tibia Vara)
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
In infantile Blount disease, excess medial pressure (such as in early walkers who are obese and
have physiologic varus alignment) produces an osteochondrosis of the physis and adjacent
epiphysis that may progress to a physeal bar.
In adolescent Blount disease, a varus moment at the knee during the stance phase of gait
further inhibits medial physeal growth according to the Hueter-Volkmann principle
(compression results in decreased growth of the physis).
Overview
Normal physiologic knee alignment includes periods of knock-knee and bowed legs5 (Figure
2).

The most common cause of pathologic genu varum is Blount disease.

Epidemiology
Affects less than 1% of the US population
Higher incidence in the African American population, females, and individuals who are obese
and those considered to walk early (before age 11 months)
Etiology
Blount disease is believed to result from biomechanical overload of the proximal
posteromedial tibial physis in individuals who are genetically susceptible.
Natural History

Tibia vara is considered physiologic in children younger than 2 years. Physiologic tibia vara
should resolve between ages 2 and 3 years.
If tibia vara is present or worsening by age 3 years, a diagnosis of Blount disease should be
considered.
The varus deformity of Blount disease is progressive if left unmanaged.
Blount disease is considered a multiplanar deformity that includes varus, procurvatum, and
internal rotation.
Risk Factors
Risk factors for infantile Blount disease
Female
Obesity
African American
Early walker (before 11 months)
Classification of Infantile Blount Disease
Langenskiöld6 described six radiographic stages that can occur over 4 to 5 years.
Early changes include metaphyseal beaking and sloping.
O Advanced changes include articular depression and medial physeal closure.
Langenskiöld stages (Figure 3)
Stage 1: medial beaking and metaphyseal irregularity (<3 years)
Stage 2: medial depression of ossification line (2 to 4 years)
Stage 3: deepening of beaking (4 to 6 years)
Stage 4: enlargement of the epiphysis; occupies depression (5 to 10 years)
Stage 5: cleft in epiphysis (8 to 11 years)
Stage 6: medial physeal closure (10 to 13 years)

Figure 3 Illustrations show the six stages of tibia vara as described by Langenskiöld. Stage I
(observed in children as old as 3 years) is characterized by medial and distal beaking of the
metaphysis and irregularity of the entire metaphysis. Stage II (observed in children aged 2.5 to 4
years) is characterized by a sharp lateromedial depression in the ossification line of the wedge-
shaped medial metaphysis. Complete restoration is common in this stage. Stage III (observed in
children aged 4 to 6 years) is characterized by deepening of the metaphyseal beak, which gives
the appearance of a step in the medial metaphysis. Stage IV (observed in children aged 5 to 10
years) is characterized by enlargement of the epiphysis, which occupies the medial metaphyseal
depression. Restoration is still possible in this stage. Stage V (observed in children aged 9 to 11
years) is characterized by a cleft in the epiphysis, which gives the appearance of a double
epiphysis; the articular surface of the medial tibia is deformed, sloping distally and medially from
the intercondylar region. Stage VI (observed in children aged 10 to 13 years) is characterized by
closure of the medial proximal tibial physis, with a normal lateral physis. Langenskiöld described
his findings based on his observations of Finnish children; changes in African American children
tend to occur at a younger age. (Reproduced from Brooks WC, Gross RH: Genu varum in children:
Diagnosis and treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1995;3[6]:326-335.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical findings suggestive of pathologic bowing include localized bowing at the proximal tibia,
severe deformity, progression, and lateral thrust during gait.7
Patient History
A thorough patient history, including age of walking, weight, nutritional allergies or special
diets, and family history of leg deformities or short stature, is important to rule out other
possible causes of tibia vara.
Surgeons should ask the patient’s parents if they consider the deformity to be progressive.
Physical Examination

Routine documentation of the patient’s height and weight to assess percentile for age
In ambulatory children, a careful examination with the patient standing and during gait
provides the most information.
Both limbs should be examined for asymmetry and alignment in frontal and sagittal planes.
The practitioner should note if the deformity is a gradual bow or an abrupt angulation.
Examination of rotational profile, including the thigh-foot angle, is essential because children
who appear to have genu varum often simply have increased tibial torsion (Figure 4).
Increased tibial torsion and procurvatum deformities often present in patients with Blount
disease.

prone on an examination table with the knees flexed at 90°. The angle of the axis of the thigh and
the axis of the foot determines internal or external tibial torsion. B, The transmalleolar axis is the
angle between a line drawn connecting the malleoli (line a-b) and the coronal plane of the tibia
(line b-c). Reproduced from Muffly BT, Muchow RD: Rotational and angular limb deformity, in
Martus JE, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Pediatrics, ed 6. Rosemont, IL: American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2022, pp 345-353.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Full-length standing radiographs from the pelvis to the feet with the patella in the forward
position should be obtained in children older than 18 months with the aforementioned

If the metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle (Figure 5) is less than 10°, a 95% likelihood exists that
the bowing will resolve.
If the metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle is greater than 16°, a 95% likelihood exists that the
bowing will progress. For metaphyseal-diaphyseal angles between 11° and 16°, monitoring is

In patients with confirmed Blount disease, assessing the Langenskiöld stage on radiographs
helps guide management.
In older patients with a more advanced Langenskiöld stage, a standing sagittal plane
radiograph of both legs with the knee in full extension is essential in identifying the degree of
procurvatum deformity.
In adolescent patients, the lateral distal femoral angle and the metaphyseal proximal tibial
angle should be carefully measured to ensure that distal femoral varus is not present

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Although MRI is not routinely indicated, it may aid in documenting the presence, size, and
location of a physeal bar in the later stages of the disease (not usually required before age 5
years).
Pathology
The histopathologic findings in the physes are the same regardless whether the child has
infantile or adolescent Blount disease.
Disorganized physeal cartilage is present with disruption of the normal architecture in the
resting zone.
Diagnosis
Tibia vara is classified as infantile if it occurs before age 5 years.
Infantile Blount disease is bilateral in 80% of patients.
Children who experience tibia vara after age 6 years are considered to have late-onset infantile
Blount disease.
Late-onset Blount disease more often occurs unilaterally and has a greater prevalence in black,
male, and obese children.
Adolescent Blount disease occurs in children older than 8 years and has a similar prevalence
profile to that of late-onset Blount disease.
Differential Diagnosis
Rickets (typically Vitamin-D resistant)
Skeletal dysplasia
Achondroplasia
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Renal osteodystrophy
Metaphyseal chondrodysplasia
Focal fibrocartilaginous dysplasia

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management of infantile Blount disease
The efficacy of brace management is controversial.
Brace management with the use of a knee-ankle-foot orthosis locked in extension may be
indicated in patients aged 2 to 3 years who have mild disease (stage 1 to stage 2).
Poor results are associated with obesity and bilaterality.
Improvement should occur within 1 year; however, management must be continued until
bony changes resolve, which usually occurs within 1.5 to 2 years.
Surgical Management
Surgical management of infantile Blount disease
Patients older than 3 years require surgical treatment.
In children younger than 3.5 years, lateral hemi-epiphysiodesis of the proximal tibia may be
considered in combination with lateral hemi-epiphysiodesis of the distal femur.
The objective is to correct the mechanical alignment of the leg as quickly as possible to allow
for more normal growth at the medial tibial plateau.
In children approaching age 4 years, a valgus tibial osteotomy is recommended, especially if
a varus thrust in gait is present.
Preoperative planning via deformity correction software is recommended to correctly
identify the apex of the deformity and plan the correction required.
This allows for accurate correction of the mechanical axis of the leg with the appropriate
translation and angulation.
To avoid recurrence, the distal fragment is fixed in slight valgus (10°), and external rotation.
For older patients, the practitioner should ensure that no procurvatum deformity is present
in the sagittal plane. If present, this should be corrected at the time of the proximal tibial
osteotomy.
Performing an anterior compartment fasciotomy at the time of surgical management
reduces the postoperative risk of compartment syndrome.
The risk of recurrence is much lower if surgical treatment is performed in children younger
than 4 years.
If a bony bar (physeal bar) is present, bar resection with interposition of fat or methyl
methacrylate is performed in combination with temporary lateral hemi-epiphysiodesis.

For patients who have severe articular incongruity and deformity, a combination of the
following should be considered:
Intra-articular osteotomy to elevate the medial plateau
Epiphysiodesis of the remaining physis
Valgus osteotomy of the tibia
Surgical management of adolescent Blount disease
Temporary or permanent hemi-epiphysiodesis of the proximal lateral tibia prevents
deformity progression and may allow for some correction in adolescents with mild to
moderate Blount disease who have at least 15 to 18 months of growth remaining.
Severe deformities and/or deformities in skeletally mature patients require proximal tibial
osteotomy.
Correction of deformity may be performed acutely or gradually via an external fixator.
Patients should be carefully assessed for distal femoral varus, which can be managed via
hemi-epiphysiodesis in immature patients or via distal femoral osteotomy in patients with
severe deformities and in mature patients.
Complications
The most common complication is recurrence, particularly in patients with alignment that was
not overcorrected by 10° and in patients older than 4 years. Patients younger than 4 years
have a 30% recurrence rate. Patients older than 4 years have a recurrence rate higher than
70%.
Compartment syndrome in the postoperative period secondary to the tibial osteotomy; can
partially be prevented by performing an anterior fasciotomy during surgical management.
Outcomes
Outcomes greatly depend on the degree of medial tibial physis involvement (Langenskiöld
classification) and the age at which treatment is initiated.
Good outcomes are directly related to overcorrection of the mechanical axis of the limb into
valgus before age 4 years.8
Posteromedial and Anteromedial Bowing
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rotational and Angular Limb Deformities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004063
17/22

Congenital posteromedial bowing often is associated with a calcaneovalgus foot. The dorsum
of the foot may be in contact with the anterior tibia in patients with this condition.
The bowing improves in the first years of life, but it rarely resolves completely.
Anteromedial bowing.
Overview
Posteromedial bowing of the tibia is a congenital deformity of the tibia with associated findings
in the foot and ankle.
Typically, spontaneous but incomplete correction of the bowing occurs within the first 4 years
of life.
Growth inhibition of the tibia remains constant.
Management focuses on addressing leg-length discrepancy if it is anticipated to be greater
than 2 cm at skeletal maturity.
The mean leg-length discrepancy without management is 3.5 cm.
Unless severe angular deformity does not correct with growth, surgical treatment is best
delayed until the patient is closer to skeletal maturity.
Epidemiology
Incidence is largely unknown.
Etiology
The cause of posteromedial bowing is unknown.
Theories include mechanical forces (the dorsiflexed foot against the tibia) and placental
abnormalities (amnion rupture).
No known genetic association
Natural History
Presents at birth
Posteromedial bowing often is confused with calcaneovalgus foot; however, the two conditions
may occur in combination or independently.
The posteromedial bow of the tibia will improve with growth, with the most rapid correction
occurring in the first year of life.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004063
18/22

Of the two methods of remodeling, reorientation of the physis contributes to greater
correction than remodeling at the diaphysis according to Wolffs law.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Monitoring for limb-length discrepancy is required. Limb-length discrepancies at maturity
usually range from 3 to 8 cm (mean, 4 cm).
Physical Examination
Calcaneovalgus foot can be differentiated from posteromedial bowing of the tibia via physical
examination.
In posteromedial bowing, the apex of deformity is in the distal tibia. Occasionally, the foot at
birth will abut the concave tibia, and a skin dimple often is present over the apex of the bow.
In calcaneovalgus foot, the apex of the deformity is at the ankle.
The two conditions can exist in combination; however, if doubt exists, a radiograph should be
obtained.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Recommended views include AP and lateral views of both tibia (for comparison), which allow
for identification of posteromedial bowing.
Bowing of the tibia improves with growth; however, a residual leg-length discrepancy persists
because of growth inhibition and may be monitored via periodic leg-length radiographs.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Initial treatment in infants begins with a stretching program of the dorsal structures of the
ankle.
Parents perform this stretching program at home after being given appropriate instructions.
Severe contractures may require serial cast immobilization for a few weeks in infancy.
The remainder of treatment focuses on managing the resulting leg-length discrepancy and
residual bowing deformity.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rotational and Angular Limb Deformities
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004063
19/22

Because the growth inhibition of the tibia remains constant, the leg-length discrepancy at
maturity can be predicted based on radiographs obtained at a young age.
Studies have shown the greater the medial bow, the greater the ultimate leg-length
discrepancy.9
Surgical Management
Management for leg-length discrepancy may involve appropriately timed contralateral
epiphysiodesis or a lengthening procedure.
The advantage of osteotomy with internal or external fixation is that any residual angular
deformity also can be addressed.
If an osteotomy is necessary, delaying surgical treatment until the patient is closer to skeletal
maturity allows for more accurate correction of the leg-length discrepancy and is associated
with a higher success rate with correction of residual deformity.
Complications
The arc of ankle range of motion remains unchanged despite surgical management.
Complications of nonsurgical management are the long-term need for an orthosis and its
associated cost.
If the leg-length discrepancy is greater than 2 cm, concern exists for the future development of
back, hip, or knee arthritis.
Complications of surgical management typically occur because of surgical correction of the leg-
length discrepancy and angular deformity.
Outcomes
The most common sequela of posteromedial bowing is a limb-length discrepancy of 3 to 4 cm
with possible limb malalignment.
